response_text: The two mechanisms work together because they utilize the same underlying context switching infrastructure but trigger via different pathways. Both cooperative yielding and pre-emptive switching eventually result in the same PendSV_Handler and osSched() functions that perform the actual thread switch - the only difference is the reason the switch is triggered. Calling osYield() for a thread sets the SVC #4 which sets the PendSV pending bit, and resets the threads runtime to its maximum timeslice value, which is how threads cooperate to yield the remaining time to the other thread or threads. When the SysTick timer expires a thread's timeslice the SysTick timer calls the same function that sets the PendSV pending bit along with resetting the runtime, but this is being done involuntarily by the thread that was pre-empted. The important take away here is both mechanisms reset a thread's runtime to its timeslice value regardless of whether it was voluntary or involuntary. Thus, a thread that yields before its run is finished gets to start with a fresh timeslice on the next time it runs. Similarly when a thread gets pre-empted it also starts with a full timeslice will be ready when it runs the next time. The scheduler does not care how a thread lost the CPU and treats all threads equally.\nThis hybrid approach provides the best of both worlds: well-behaved threads can yield immediately when they finish their work (improving system responsiveness), while misbehaving threads that never yield still get forcibly switched after their timeslice expires (maintaining system fairness). The OS doesn't need separate scheduling queues or different context switching mechanisms - it simply uses different triggers for the same underlying thread switching process.\n
